otherNames: Constantine the Philosopher, Cyril's name until he took the name Cyril in Rome, by the Italian Legend
knownFor: Two brothers of Thessalonica who taught the Slavs of Moravia the faith in their own language. Pope John VIII praised the Slavonic letters found by Constantine and, in 880, allowed the Mass to be sung in Slavonic, with the Gospel read first in Latin.
datesNote: Ninth century. No source used here gives either brother's year of birth. Johann Ginzel reckons their arrival in Moravia to 863. Cyril died in Rome on 14 February, by the Italian Legend; Ginzel accepts 868 for the year, and Ernst Dümmler and S. H. Cross give 869. Methodius died on 6 April, in the year 6393 from the creation, by the Life of Methodius; Ginzel works this out as 885
placeNote: Thessalonica, their home; Cherson, where the Italian Legend says Constantine found the relics of Clement of Rome; Moravia, their mission; Rome, where Cyril died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Clement; Pannonia, the see Methodius was made bishop for, by the Life of Methodius
role: Brothers and missionaries: Constantine (Cyril), priest, scholar and finder of the Slavonic letters; Methodius, monk, then bishop and archbishop for the Slavs

keyWorks.title: The Slavonic letters
keyWorks.about: which Pope John VIII calls the Slavonic letters found by Constantine the Philosopher. S. H. Cross says Constantine made the Glagolitic letters, not the Cyrillic; Count Lützow says his alphabet became known as Cyrillic

keyWorks.title: Slavonic translations
keyWorks.about: the Gospel, the Apostle, the Psalter and chosen services, by the two brothers, as the Life of Methodius says; it adds that Methodius later put the rest of the Scriptures into Slavonic in six months

traces: The Russian Primary Chronicle says the writing made for Moravia exists also in Rus and among the Danube Bulgarians.
The Life of Clement of Ohrid names Gorazd, Clement, Naum, Angelarius and Sava as the brothers' chief disciples.
The Life of Methodius says he named Gorazd, a man of the Moravians' own country, learned in Latin books, to follow him.
remembered: In S. H. Cross's English of the Russian Primary Chronicle, "The Slavs rejoiced to hear the greatness of God extolled in their native tongue."
Ginzel reports that in 1380 Bishop John of Olomouc ordered their feast kept on 9 March, as Moravia's chief fathers, apostles and patrons.

Augustin Theiner dedicated his Vatican documents of 1863 to Joseph George Strossmayer, bishop of Bosnia or Diakovo, and wrote that the work kept the thousandth-year feast of Saints Cyril and Methodius, which the Church celebrated that year.

uncertain: Which account to trust. Ginzel trusts the Italian Legend, which the Bollandists, and Ginzel after them, think very probably the work of Gauderich of Velletri, a bishop of the brothers' time. Of the Life of Methodius, Dümmler says a pupil wrote it soon after Methodius died, and Wilhelm Wattenbach rates it highly. Ginzel, who writes against the Greek schism, calls it a Greek schismatic's concoction.

Who made them bishops. The Italian Legend says Pope Hadrian II made both brothers bishops. The Life of Methodius says Pope Nicholas received them and ordained Methodius priest, and that he was made bishop later, for the Slavs of Pannonia.
How long they stayed in Moravia. The Italian Legend says four and a half years; the Life of Methodius says three. Ginzel follows the Legend and calls the Life wrong.
The year Cyril died. Ginzel accepts 868; Dümmler and Cross give 869.
The day Methodius died. The Life gives 6 April, in the year Ginzel works out as 885. Ginzel reports that Wattenbach thought a death on so high a feast suspicious, and defends the date.

His prison. The Life of Methodius says the enemy of the Moravian king and all the bishops sent him to Swabia and held him two and a half years. Count Lützow says the German governors seized him and handed him as a prisoner to the German bishops. Only the Life gives the place and the length.
The six-month Bible. Cross says it is generally regarded as apocryphal.
The Salzburg account against Methodius is hostile. Ginzel and Bartholomäus Kopitar date it to 873; Ginzel reports that Joseph Assemani and Wattenbach give 871.

briefReferences: Life of Constantine, lines 20217–20233: Moravia asks for a teacher in its own language; the emperor sends the tired philosopher; "if they have letters for their language"; "who can write words on water"; the letters made after prayer.
Life of Methodius, lines 12201–12219: Rastislav's embassy, with teachers from Italy, Greece and Germany; the emperor's word that all Thessalonians speak pure Slavonic; the letters made.
Life of Constantine, lines 20256–20268: the services turned into Slavic; the Latin clergy who said God chose only three languages.
Life of Constantine, lines 20292–20314: Venice, the Latin bishops, priests and monks, and his answer.
Life of Constantine, lines 20379–20445: Rome, the pope comes out to meet them with Clement's relics; his illness; the monk's name Cyril; his death on 14 February, aged 42.
Life of Methodius, lines 12249–12365: his last words to Methodius, and his plea not to give up his teaching for the mountain; Methodius bishop for Pannonia; held two and a half years in Swabia.
Salzburg Conversio: the "Greek" with "newly invented Slavic letters" who partly cheapened the Latin Masses and Gospels.
Pope John VIII, letter of 879 to Methodius: the earlier ban on Slavonic Mass repeated, with preaching in Slavonic still allowed.
Pope John VIII, letter of 880 to Svatopluk: the Slavonic letters found by Constantine, Slavonic Mass allowed, the Gospel read first in Latin, and the three chief languages.

Life of Methodius, lines 12540–12551; his death on 6 April; the funeral in Latin, Greek and Slavonic, with crowds rich and poor, free and slave; Lützow for 885. Life of Clement (Latin extract in Ginzel): Wiching set up, the disciples driven out.

Life of Clement, PG 126: the younger priests and deacons sold, the teachers chained, then stripped and driven out; Clement, Naum and Angelarius to Bulgaria; Boris thanks God; Clement "the first bishop of the Bulgarian tongue"; the plain sermons.
Editor's note to the Life of Clement, PG 126: its author says he lived with Clement and was Bulgarian, though the work carries Theophylact's name.
Lützow, Bohemia: Rostislav's mission to Constantinople in 862, for the 860s.
Russian Primary Chronicle, tr. Cross: the writing first made for the Moravians, found in Rus and among the Danube Bulgarians; Cross's introduction for 869 and the dating.
Dümmler's introduction to the Life of Constantine and Ginzel on the Life of Methodius: the Lives written by followers, kept in late copies.
World census, Cyrillo-Methodian Slavic Christianity: their tradition, and the Czech Republic for Moravia.
